display_title: Okay submission. Imformative and Sound Experiment Results

content.title: Okay submission. Imformative and Sound Experiment Results
content.review:
### Overall
This work presents a new DNNs pruning method, Pruning with Energy Distance (PED). This method works based on the energy distance between hidden-layer output and the final representation learned from the DNNs. Imformative experiments show that PED outperforms those existing SOTA compression methods on various benchmark datasets.

### Pros
1) This work supports the merits of PED with plenty of experiment results. They compare PED with several SOTA methods to show the outstanding performance. 
2) This work proposes the energy distance (ED) as the knowledge for the pruning. Such method does not rely on the pre-knowledge of feature distribution in the dataset, and all the pruning knowledge is learned automatically.

### Cons
1) The overall submission is okay. Readers can get the rough idea of PED. However, it seems not ready enough for a submission in the conference. Typos show that some parts of this work haven't went through proof reading. For example, in page 5, the last 10th line, "Please see section ?? in the". The reader could get the content in the appendix, but it should be fixed a more clear description. Another example is the number in tables. In table 4, the Top1 Acc of HRand Lin et a. (2020) should be "0.7198" not "0.71.98". More examples, "Next PED uses \hat{D}" in page 4 could be "Next, PED uses \hat{D}".
2) The section of "Proposed Algorithm" is trying to explain the main idea of PED, but it is hard for readers to follow. Notations are mixed in the description how PED works. Since the organization of section 3.2 looks clear, I suggest the authors rewrite or at least re-organize the section 3.3 to make the section 3 more readable. For example, those notations K, A, S could be introduced before the formal description. Since the main idea will be shown in Algorithm1, readers would like to know more intuition of this algorithm. Authors would not need to show the steps in the content but leave the key steps only. Things like how to do the clustering can be moved to footnotes. The analysis of experiment results could be moved to section 4. 
3) Although the model compression method focuses on how to reduce the inference complexity of DNNs, an expensive pruning method is still painful in practice. I would suggest this work presenting time complexity analysis for PED compared to SOTA method. And since the algorithm mentions Train_err multiple time, the definition of such notation should be clear in advance. After following the description, we are still wondering how and when to compute such Train_err. Do the users need to compute the Train_err for the whole datasets? Does the Train_err require the user to train the pruned model until converge? And the algorithm requires to get the min candidate in centroids. Will the computation power be consumed for unused candidate if the method really needs long training process?
4) Minor issues: Figure 2 could be re-draw to fit the page limit. The presented one is too flat to show the difference between curves and the legends are too flat as well. 
5) Missing reference: Dai, Bin, et al. "Compressing neural networks using the variational information bottleneck." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2018. This work also mention how to utilize mutual information in the compression scenario.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Explaining Train_err, fixing typos, organizing sections, and discussion about the referred paper

content.title: Explaining Train_err, fixing typos, organizing sections, and discussion about the referred paper
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedbacks.

First, we thank you for your encouraging comments. We apologize that some of the existing typos made reading the submitted draft difficult. We have fixed all such issues and cleaned the paper. In addition, per your request, we have represented section 3.3 in a more readable way by defining the symbols in the algorithm, and description of the algorithm in different parts.  We have also changed the figure 2 to fit the page limit, so it is not flat anymore. Please see the updated version of the paper.

Regarding the Train_err in the algorithm, we have to mention that the Train_err is used for choosing the best cluster number. As mentioned in section 3.3, $K^t$ is a set that includes the candidates for the number of clusters at stage $t$. Here, Train_err is referred to as the error of the pruned model with $k\in K^t$ clusters. For example, let $K^t= [10, 11, 12, 13]$ be the cluster vector at stage $t$, then we compute the errors of the pruned model respectively with 10, 11, 12, and 13 clusters by feeding the model with training samples. Hence, we obtain 4 numbers out of which we select the minimum one and its corresponding cluster number, which we call as $k^t_*$. As you can see, we don't train anything here, this is just simply passing training samples and compute the loss (just forward pass and no backward at all); hence, it is quite fast. In this way, we can select the model with the minimum hurt to the performance. Once we decided on the model with $k^t_*$ at stage $t$, we re-train the model with $k_*^t$ units with the weights initialized from the previous stage. This is the end of the stage $t$. 

Regarding the missing paper by Dai, Bin, et al, 2018, we first thank the reviewer for pointing out this paper and we will add this paper to the reference. However, comparing this paper with ours is hard for two specific reasons: first, the paper by Dai, Bin, et al, 2018 is about using mutual information (MI) for compressing the deep models, while we do not use MI for the reasons discussed in Section 3.2, and indeed these reasons were our motivation to look for a model-free measure. Next and more importantly, the focus of the approach by Dai, Bin, et al, 2018 is not pruning models with skip-connections (e.g., ResNet and DenseNet), and as opposed to our approach, the pruning is not done at the level of units. We need to mention that our approach is based on the energy distance between the hidden units (defined in the paper as a set of several layers) $\textbf{not the hidden-layers}$ and the final representation learned from the DNNs. Beyond all these points, this paper does not provide any experiments for ImageNet data sets and ResNet models which makes it even harder to be compared with the SOTA approaches and our method. In our paper, we have compared with the other methods and baselines based on 3 factors of being the SOTA, relevance to our paper, and reported different criteria. In addition, we have compared with any related paper we were aware of at the submission time. The most related ones are BlockDrop by Wu et al. 2018, and SkipNet by Wang et al. 2018 where we have included in Tables 1 and 2.

content.title: Model-Free Energy Distance for Pruning DNNs
content.review: This paper introduces a metric called "energy distance" in DNN pruning to evaluate the relationship between feature maps and the output. However, the rationale behind this metric is not clear. The definition and discussions of this metric in Section 3.2 are inconsistent with the way it is used in Section 3.3, making the validity of the former definition unconvincing. Besides, since the results in this paper show that the maximum value of this metric does not mean the best pruning effect, what changes have been made to this metric to get the best pruning effect need to be explained. Thus, it is hard to tell whether this metric is really effective and the improvement shown in the experiments seems marginal. Additionally, the organization of experimental results needs to be improved. As this paper aims at proposing a new pruning method, it is suggested to put results from the same model together when comparing algorithms. Besides, as the main contribution is a new metric for network pruning, it is necessary to compare different metrics and put their comparison results together.

display_title: Intuition behind the energy distance and energy dependence, reorganizing the results

content.title: Intuition behind the energy distance and energy dependence, reorganizing the results
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedbacks.

We need to clarify some points. First, we note that we have two concepts: one is the $\textbf{Energy Distance}$ and its estimated version, and the second concept is $\textbf{ Energy Dependence}$ and its estimated version.  These concepts have been clearly explained with different notations in the paper. Energy Distance is given by Definition 1 is denoted by $\mathcal{E}(F_1, F_2)$, while its consistent and unbiased estimation is given by equation 6 and denoted by $\hat{\mathcal{E}}(F_1,F_2)$. Please note that in Definition 1, we have said that the Energy Distance between two continuous-valued random vectors with CDF $F_1$ and $F_2$. On the other hand, in classification problems such as the one in our paper, the second CDF (CDF of the output of the model) needs to be a categorical (discrete) distribution with $p$ categories. Hence, we introduced ``$\textbf{Energy Dependence}$ in $\textbf{Definition 2}$ to account for pair of continuous-discrete random variables/vectors. Specifically, we defined the Energy Dependence in Definition 2 based on the maximum of the energy distance between conditional distributions, $(T|Y=i)\sim F_i$ and $(T|Y=j)\sim F_j$ for $1 \leq i,j \leq p$. Please note that since in practice the estimated version of Energy Distance should be used (i.e., $\hat{\mathcal{E}}(F_1, F_2)$), we also  have to use the estimated version of Energy Dependence, $\hat{D}(T,Y)$ instead of $D(T,Y)$ which is given by $\hat{D}(T,Y) = \max_{1\leq i,j \leq p} \hat{\mathcal{E}}(F_1,F_2)$. We have mentioned this point at the fourth footnote on page 4. We kindly ask the reviewer to explain and make more clear which is inconsistent with the definition of Energy Distance in sections 3.2 and 3.3 as we think that we were clear about these concepts. 

Regarding the maximum value of Energy Distance, we have to mention that our rationale to define the Energy Dependence in Definition 2 between the units (not the layers) and the output of the model is to $\textbf{maximize the discrepancy between two distributions}$. This intuition is coming from the Shannon Mutual Information (MI) as a natural and mathematical appealing tool for measuring the information learned by the feature maps at the level of units. This means that the larger the information between two random variables, the more information between them. However,  as discussed at the beginning of section 3.2, MI is hard to be estimated for the high-dimensional space of feature maps. Hence, we came up with the energy distance as a measure of information that does not only enjoy the properties of MI, but it can easily be computed even in the high-dimension of the space of feature maps. Based on the above discussion, the maximum of the energy distance between conditional distributions implies maximum discrepancy between two distributions; hence maximum energy (information). 
 

We have also rearranged the results in the revised paper to show the same and similar models together.  Finally, we are not aware of any paper in the pruning literature that has used the notion of information for making a decision about the redundancy of the units or even layers. The only paper is due to Dai, Bin, et al, 2018 which is about using mutual information for compressing the deep models. However, this paper is not about skip-connection models, and pruning in the level of units, and more importantly is not even considered as the SOTA (even it does not have any ImageNet results). This paper does not have any experiments with the models with the skip-connections. Given all this, the comparison with this paper is very hard. We'd be happy if you the reviewer can refer us to some papers about compression of NN where the approach is similar to ours and use the notion of information, so we can compare and include them in our paper.

content.title: Pruning with Energy distance
content.review:
This paper proposes a method of finding an informative layer of a network by energy distance and performing pruning based on this. There are some new aspects to finding informative layers in a non-parametric way. 
However, this paper is not yet ready for publication for the following reasons.

- Limited contribution of Energy Dependence to performance\
Figure 2 shows the difference in performance between random and the proposed method is limited, especially for reduction range 0% to 60%. In particular, the reduction rates of the experimental results in this paper are mostly within 60%. How many times were each experiment performed for the results in Figure 2?

- Unfair comparison\
It is difficult to understand why Cutout augmentation is used in Cifar experiments.
Retraining is performed by repeating a large number of stages, and it is difficult to exclude the gain due to this training budget increase.
For example, in [1] , even if the author re-initializes [2] and uses the same training budget, the result was 73.41% with ResNet50. This is a higher accuracy than this paper.\
[1] Rethinking the value of network pruning, Z. Liu\
[2] Data-driven sparse structure selection for deep neural networks, Z. Huang

- Omission of some high performance baselines\
[1] Convolutional Networks with Adaptive Inference Graphs, A. Veit\
[2] Autopruner: An end-to-end trainable filter pruning method for efficient deep model inference, J. Luo\
[3] URNet : User-Resizable Residual Networks with Conditional Gating Module, S. Lee\
[4] Channel selection using Gumbel Softmax, C. Herrmann

- Missing important experimental settings \
Re-train is performed during N stages, but the paper does not include essential hyper-parameters such as training epoch and learning rate.

- Many writing errors \
Page 1, "ReseNet"\
Page 5, refers to the appendix, which is not included.\
"Section ??"
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

display_title: Details of experiments, limitation of the proposed method, comparison with other approaches

content.title: Details of experiments, limitation of the proposed method, comparison with other approaches
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments. 

Please kindly recall that we are not removing just uninformative layers--we are removing uninformative units as defined in the paper. So unfortunately the summary is inaccurate. 

Additionally, we have provided all the details of the experiments in the appendix. We have reported the number of epochs,  learning rate, scheduling for diminishing the learning rate, the weight decay, and other things in Sections A.1, A.6, and A.6.7 for CIFAR-10/100 and SVHN, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet, respectively. The 8 pages limit makes it impossible to mention all the details of every experiment. This is the reason that numerous papers push the details of implementations to the appendix in order to use the main space for discussing the approach, concept, and algorithm Moreover, we have made our code publicly available for anyone interested in reproducing the results. So, every information about the details is available.

For the comparison that you mentioned, we have included almost 80 reference papers and compared our approach with the SOTA methods which we were aware of. We cannot compare with everything in the literature, and thus have selected the baseline papers based on 3 factors of being the SOTA,  relevance to our paper, reported different criteria, etc. In fact,  in the second, third, and fourth paper that you pointed out, there is no reported compression ratio in terms of the number of parameters. This is simply because these approaches are structured, and probably do not have good performance in terms of pruned number of parameters; hence, they only report FLOPs count which is in general not a reliable measure as different papers consider different ways to count FLOPs (this is not the case for the parameters count). We have discussed these points in the paper (see the footnote on page 7 and discussion in section2 on page 2). The first paper by A. Viet is not even considered as the SOTA method and this paper and ours are not comparable. In Table 1 (for CIFAR10), in the best case, the method of this paper achieves 94.86% accuracy with 1.7 million parameters. However, our approach can get far better performance: 95.19% accuracy with 0.48 million parameters for ResNet164 which originally has 1.7 million parameters similar to the ConvNet-AIG 110*. Also, in Table 2 for ImageNet of this paper, the performance is far less than ours in terms of the number of parameters. Our algorithm, PED can reduce the parameters of ResNet50 from 26 million to 12.4 million (more than 51% reduction), while ConvNet-AIG 50 [t=0.7]  model in A.Viet has 26 million parameters. The second paper by J. Luo is again not comparable to our approach since it does pruning at the level of filters, not at the unit level like us. Moreover, it has not reported any gain in terms of the number of parameters which makes the comparison even harder.  While the third paper by S. Lee is dealing with the residual units, they are limited only to this family. While our approach is dealing with any skip-connection models such as DenseNet ones. Plus, it is hard to compare the results of this paper to our method as this paper doesn't have anything reported in terms of the number of parameters. The last paper by C. Herrmann prunes at the level of filters (not at the level units). Also, it doesn't report any gains in terms of pruned number of parameters.  

For the Cutout, this is just a training technique and nothing to do with the test data set. We wanted to see the effect of different training techniques in the final pruning performance. We also have experiments in which we have not used the Cutout (SVHN and ImageNet). Also, we have tried for ourselves the CIFARs experiments without Cutout in training the full model, and have not observed any performance degradation. For the paper by Z. Liu, we are not sure how you claim this number and just consider the 73.41% and not the pruned number of parameters. In deep compression, accuracy is not the only criterion. There is a trade-off between accuracy, parameter counts, and FLOPs. Also, our approach is based on multi-stages training as we have mentioned this in the paper. Plus, 6 to 10 stages are not a "large number". The whole point of deep compression is to come up with a model probably offline and before deployment. Also, many other pruning approaches follow this retraining strategy.

For the random scheme, we think there is a misconception. The x-axis is the remaining parameters/FLOPs, so the gap between the proposed approach and the random one increases after 55% pruned parameters and 60% pruned for FLOPs. This is indeed an interesting observation, not a limitation that says for achieving a higher rate compression, simple random dropping is not a good strategy. A good compression method is the one with a higher compression rate. We have also run the random scheme 3 times. We will add the experiment with 10 runs and report the average of them.

We have fixed the typos you have mentioned.

content.review:
This paper presents one new framework for model compression. The comparison between the feature map of skip-connections and the model output is used as the criteria for model compression. However, the description of the approach is not very clear in details, it may help people understand better with figure diagram along with the workflow. Perhaps the author can consider showing one example of how D can be calculated. This approach belongs to structured model compression. It seems that it is only limited the network with skip-connection.  It would be good to see the extension of this idea to other general network without skip-connections.  There are several typos in the paper, e.g., 
a. in Theorem, it should be 'if' instead of "iff". 
b. please see section ?? at the paragraph before Section 4. 
The legends in Figure 1 and 2 are also not very easy to read.

display_title: Limited to the network with skip-connection and Energy Dependence (D) computation

content.title: Limited to the network with skip-connection and Energy Dependence (D) computation
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable feedbacks. 

Regarding your comment about the limitation of this approach to the network with the skip-connection, we need to clarify some points. First, On page 1 in the "Our Contributions" part,  we have clearly mentioned that our focus in this paper is on pruning the network with skip-connection (e.g. ResNet and DenseNet families).  In fact, many papers in deep network compression literature have only focused on the residual networks(e.g., BlockDrop by  Wu et al. 2018, and SkipNet by Wang et al. 2018).  The motivation for all these papers is the observation reported by Veit et al., 2016. We have mentioned this point at the beginning of section 3.1 on page 2. 

Our approach is applicable to any model which has skip-connection(s) not only the ResNet models. In addition, almost all the modern networks which have remarkable performance in various computer vision and NLP  tasks use the architectural design inspired by ResNet (having skip-connection(s)). The idea of having skip-connection is not only used in supervised tasks,  but also in the generative models with impressive performance such as BigGAN (Andrew et al., 2018).

In this paper, our goal is to investigate the robustness of the skip-connection models in terms of removing/pruning a set of layers not only individual layers in a more systematic way. As pointed out on page 1 in section 3.1 and by Veit et al., 2016., this is not the case for sequential networks such as VGG, AlexNet, etc. Given all these observations, we don't think that this is a limitation as we are clear about our goal in this paper. Finally, studying the proposed approach for the other models and even unstructured methods can be an interesting research direction; however, our goal here is to study very commonly used and spread skip-connection models in the literature.

For computing D, in section 3.3, we have mentioned that our proposed algorithm, PED computes D using Definition 2 and Equation 6. As discussed in the line above the equation 6, for computing D between a unit i and the output, we only need the samples for both of these random variables as D is computed only by the Euclidean distance between these samples. All the samples are easily available by passing the input images through the model and reading the feature maps from each unit (Computing D is simply given by the sum of differences between samples).  In addition, we have also provided four plots in Figure 1 to illustrate the values of D across different stages of the proposed pruning algorithm. 

We have fixed the typos you have mentioned ('iff' , "section ??"). Also, we have reworded the captions for Figures 1 and 2 to be read better.
